A glassmaker from Staffordshire who came to Salem in the 1630s, among the first to make glass in New England.
In the 1650s he and his wife Cassandra became Quakers.
The Massachusetts authorities fined, jailed and whipped them for it, and when the court ordered their children Daniel
and Provided sold in Barbados to pay the family's fines, no ship's master in Salem would carry them.
In 1659 Lawrence and Cassandra were banished on pain of death.
They found refuge on Shelter Island, New York, and both died there the following year.
Wife of Lawrence Southwick of Salem. With him she was fined, imprisoned and whipped for her Quaker faith,
and banished in 1659; they died within days of each other on Shelter Island in 1660.
John Greenleaf Whittier's poem "Cassandra Southwick" (1843) gave her name to the story of her daughter Provided,
whom the court had ordered sold.
